title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, and Risk Exceptions
author: Asha Patel
body:
Summary:

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's primary security and compliance controls related to: RBAC and authentication, centralized audit logging, data residency and retention policies, the secure software development lifecycle (Secure SDLC), security-oriented incident response procedures, compliance evidence workflows for audits (SOC 2 / ISO 27001), and the risk & exceptions process. It is intended for system owners, engineering leads, product managers, security reviewers, and audit owners.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to all Redwood-managed systems and services across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
- Customer-specific contractual requirements (data residency or retention) live in the customer contract and override default policies; see the "Customer Data Contracts" section in product-docs.

Owners and contacts:
- Policy owner: Security (policy owner: Asha Patel, security@redwood.example.com)
- Evidence owner (audits): Compliance Team (compliance@redwood.example.com)
- On-call security responder: see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-and-incident-response for rotation and pager contacts.

1) RBAC and Authentication (Overview)

Goals:
- Principle of least privilege (PoLP) enforced across cloud console, internal services, and the Redwood Console.
- Centralized identity provider for authentication, automated provisioning/deprovisioning, and fine-grained authorization for service-to-service and human actors.

Core controls and operational rules:
- Identity Provider: Okta (OIDC + SAML) is the canonical IdP for Redwood. All employees and contractors must authenticate via SSO.
- Provisioning: SCIM-based automated provisioning from Workday to Okta for employee lifecycle. Manual exceptions require manager and People Ops approval and are documented in the HR ticket.
- MFA: Required for all interactive accounts. Hardware-backed FIDO2 keys are the recommended default; TOTP is allowed as second factor for contractor accounts.
- Authentication session policies: interactive sessions expire after 8 hours of inactivity; high-privilege operations (admin role changes, KMS key rotations, production secrets creation) require re-auth within 4 hours.
- Password policy: not applicable for SSO-managed accounts; service accounts with long-lived credentials must be rotated every 90 days and use short-lived tokens where possible.

RBAC model and roles (canonical):
- roles: ["viewer", "developer", "service-account", "operator", "security-auditor", "admin", "compliance"]
- Permission mapping (examples):
  - viewer: read-only to dashboards, docs, and monitoring; no write to infra.
  - developer: code commit, CI job triggers, non-production deploy.
  - operator: production deploy, runbooks execution, incident triage access.
  - admin: global tenant and infra management (rare; requires two-person approval).
  - security-auditor: read-only access to audit logs and config snapshots; no deployment privileges.
  - service-account: scoped API permissions with least privilege; bound to named owners and linked to automation tickets.

Service-level enforcements:
- GitOps repositories are protected with branch rules; admin merge requires two approvers for prod branches and must include a security reviewer for infra changes.
- Kubernetes RBAC is mapped from central IAM groups and reviewed quarterly.
- KMS/HSM access is restricted to required operator roles and audited on each use.

Onboarding / Offboarding procedures:
1. New hire onboarding triggers: create Okta account, add to groups based on role, provision GitHub and cloud roles (least-privilege templates).
2. Offboarding: immediate Okta deactivation on termination; automated revocation of sessions and tokens via SCIM and cloud governance playbooks; follow-up validation within 24 hours by HR and Security.

2) Audit Logging (Design & Operational Requirements)

Purpose: Provide immutable, queryable records for security events, admin actions, data access, configuration changes, and API activity to support incident response, forensics, and compliance.

Sources & collection:
- Sources: API gateway logs, application audit trails (Redwood API), control plane events, KMS key usage logs, IAM changes, database access logs, host/system logs, and CI/CD pipeline events.
- Collector service: AuditLogService (agent on hosts + centralized collectors). Logs are forwarded over TLS to the ingestion pipeline (Kafka -> processing -> cold storage).

Storage and retention (default):
| Data class           | Storage location (default)                      | Retention |
|----------------------|--------------------------------------------------|-----------|
| Admin & config logs  | s3://redwood-audit-logs-prod (encrypted @KMS)   | 7 years   |
| Access logs (app/API)| es/Datadog indices -> archived to S3             | 3 years   |
| System & debug logs  | Hot indices (24/7) -> archived after 90 days    | 90 days   |
| Security alerts      | SIEM (Splunk/Datadog) + archive to S3           | 7 years   |

- Data residency: audit logs are stored in-region for EU customers (s3://redwood-audit-logs-eu) and in the US for US customers. Cross-region forwarding requires a documented, approved exception.
- Tamper-evidence: All audit records are signed with a write-only KMS key and checksummed on ingestion. Append-only storage with object immutability enabled for production buckets.

Access and monitoring:
- Security: read-only audit access via "security-auditor" role. Admin-level access to change logging config requires two-person approval and is itself logged.
- Alerts: anomalous behavior (large bulk downloads, unusual KMS key usage, mass permission grants) generate automated incidents to PagerDuty security-oncall.
- SLOs: audit ingestion latency <= 2 minutes for critical events, 95th percentile; missed ingestion incidents are treated as S1 until recovered.

3) Data Residency & Retention (Policy)

Principles:
- Default storage region follows customer region selection. Customer contracts may specify strict residency requirements — comply with contract and escalate to Legal & Security for ambiguous requirements.
- Minimize cross-border data transfer. When cross-border transfer is required (third-party services), enforce contractual safeguards (SCCs or equivalent).

Data classification and retention (default policy):
- Customer Personal Data (PII): retained as contractually required; default retention 7 years for compliance-sensitive datasets. Disposal processes must be cryptographically-secure (crypto-wipe).
- Customer Non-PII (analytics): default retention 2 years, subject to configurable retention per customer in the Console.
- Audit logs & security evidence: 7 years (see Audit Logging).
- Backups and snapshots: retention varies by environment; production DB snapshots default to 90 days unless contractually instructed otherwise.

Encryption & KMS:
- At-rest encryption enforced for all customer data using KMS-managed keys. For Private deployments, customers may supply KMS keys (BYOK) and Redwood will integrate via standard KMS protocols.
- In-transit TLS 1.2+ enforced for all network traffic.

Residency controls for Private and Dedicated deployments:
- Private (VPC/on-prem): customers control network boundaries and storage; Redwood provides an integration checklist for validating local logs, backups, and key custody.
- Dedicated: Redwood operator configures region-local storage by default; cross-region replication requires documented approval.

4) Secure SDLC (Controls & Gates)

Objectives:
- Shift security left: threat modeling, dependency scanning, and secure design during design and PR phases.
- Maintain traceable security sign-off before production deploys.

Minimum pipeline controls:
- SAST/SCA: All PRs must pass static analysis (Snyk for dependencies, Semgrep rules for code patterns).
- Secret scanning: Gitleaks scans on push; CI fails if secrets are detected.
- Test coverage & CI gates: builds must pass unit tests and integration smoke tests; recommended minimum branch coverage 70% (team-specific higher targets encouraged).
- Infrastructure as Code: Terraform plans require a security reviewer for IAM/KMS/network changes; all plans are executed via CI with drift detection.
- Container security: images are scanned for vulnerabilities during CI and stored in private registry with immutable tags.
- Feature flags & canary: production releases use feature flags for risky changes and staged canary rollouts (10% -> 50% -> 100%).

Design & review rituals:
- Threat modeling: required for any new external-facing service, data store changes that expand data scope, or changes to auth controls. Approved threat model artifacts must be attached to the PR.
- Security review: changes that touch auth, KMS, PCI, or data-retention must include Security reviewer approval before merge.

Production deployment sign-off:
- The deploy checklist includes QA sign-off, monitoring instrumentation (metrics and alerts), runbook link, rollback plan, and security owner approval for privileged changes.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Severity classification (examples):
- S1 (Critical): confirmed PII exfiltration, active compromised private keys/KMS keys, production data destruction, or persistent control-plane compromise.
- S2 (High): unauthorized access to non-PII customer data, infrastructure-level compromises with limited blast radius.
- S3 (Medium): application errors exposing small datasets or degraded monitoring.
- S4 (Low): informational events or policy violations with no user impact.

High-level playbook (S1 example):
1. Detection & Triage (0-15 minutes): First responder (on-call security) categorizes event and assigns incident commander.
2. Containment (15-60 minutes): Isolate affected systems (network ACLs, revoke exposed credentials, rotate affected service accounts).
3. Forensics & Evidence Preservation (1-6 hours): Snapshot affected systems, preserve audit logs in write-once storage, capture memory if required, and record chain of custody in the incident ticket.
4. Eradication & Recovery (6-72 hours): Patch/remediate root cause, validate with tests, and restore services from known-good snapshots.
5. Customer & Regulator Communication (within 72 hours for qualifying PII breaches): Coordinate with Legal and Customer Success to notify affected customers and regulators as required by law and contract.
6. Post-incident Review (2 weeks): Publish a blameless postmortem with timeline, impact, root cause, mitigations, and owners for follow-up actions; track actions until completion.

Operational details and tooling:
- Incident tracking: Jira security-incident project with dedicated templates.
- Evidence capture: use AuditLogService exports and Confluence incident pages; evidence artifacts are stored in s3://redwood-incident-evidence-prod with restricted access.
- Pager mechanisms: PagerDuty for escalation; Slack incident channel created automatically by incident orchestration bot; security-oncall must acknowledge within 15 minutes for S1 incidents.

Regulatory notification thresholds and timelines:
- GDPR: notify supervisory authority within 72 hours for personal data breaches where required.
- Contractual/regional obligations: follow timelines defined per customer contracts; default notification target is 72 hours for qualifying incidents.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows (Audits)

Applicable frameworks: SOC 2 Type II (primary), ISO 27001 (selected customers), and supporting attestations (pen-test reports, encryption attestations).

Annual (or ad-hoc) audit workflow:
1. Pre-audit collection: Compliance team issues an Evidence Request (ER) via the ComplianceEvidenceService with a deadline.
2. Evidence owners (system/service owners) gather artifacts: configuration snapshots, policy documents, runbooks, access lists, training records, and signing logs.
3. Store artifacts: Evidence uploaded to the Compliance evidence repository (encrypted S3 + Confluence links). Each artifact must list owner, retention date, and hash for integrity verification.
4. Internal readiness review: Compliance performs a gap analysis and returns a remediation list.
5. External auditor engagement: provide access to read-only views and compiled evidence bundles.
6. Post-audit actions: remediate findings, update policies, and close audit observations within agreed SLAs (typically 90 days).

Evidence retention: Minimum 7 years for SOC2/ISO artifacts tied to controls; shorter retention allowed if contractually specified and approved.

7) Risk & Exceptions Process

Purpose: Track, approve, and monitor exceptions to baseline security controls when compensating controls are in place or transitional constraints exist.

Exception request requirements:
- Required fields: service(s) affected, control(s) being exempted, justification, compensating controls, duration requested (max 180 days without explicit RAB approval for longer), business owner, security sponsor, and rollback plan.
- Submission path: create a Risk Exception Request in the risk register (Jira project: RISK) and attach technical evidence.

Approval and governance:
- Risk Acceptance Board (RAB): meets weekly; includes Security, Legal, Engineering Leadership, and a Compliance representative.
- Short-lived exceptions (<30 days) may be approved by Security + Engineering manager with post-facto RAB notification.
- All exceptions require quarterly reviews and a sunset plan; exceptions without active mitigation are revoked automatically at expiration.

Compensating controls examples:
- If an endpoint requires elevated permissions temporarily, require network segmentation, time-bound tokens, session monitoring, and enhanced audit sampling.
- For third-party service that stores EU data temporarily, require encrypted-at-rest, access restrictions, and SCC-signed contract addendum.

Risk register & metrics:
- Each approved exception is logged in the central risk register with owner, approval date, expiration, and status.
- Security reports to the executive team monthly: number of open exceptions, time-to-remediation, and top residual risks.
